newsitem.title: USA: Blood marker linked to Tourettes, study says.
newsitem.headline: Blood marker linked to Tourettes, study says.

text.p: Abnormally high levels of a certain protein in the blood have been linked to obsessive-compulsive disorder and Tourette's syndrome, researchers at the University of Florida said.
Researchers at the university's College of Medicine said in a statement Saturday that the finding could lead to a simple blood test to determine whether patients are predisposed to the disorders.

In a test group of 31 patients who had either childhood-onset obsessive-compulsive disorder or Tourette's Syndrome, all had unusually high levels of the antigen known as D8/17. In a control group of 21 healthy participants, only one displayed unusual levels of the marker protein.

More than 5 million people in the United States suffer from obsessive-compulsive disorder, characterized by unwanted fears of such things as contamination. The obsessions lead to compulsive behaviors such as repeated handwashing or wiping clean door handles.

Tourette's syndrome affects more than 200,000 people in the United States. Once considered an emotional illness, it is now understood to be a neurological disease characterized by involuntary muscular tics, such as eye twitching, head jerking and grimaces, along with socially awkward snorting, throat noises and involuntary outbursts of obscenities.

The Florida study, reported in the current issue of the American Journal of Psychiatry, strengthens evidence that Tourette's and some forms of obsessive-compulsive disorder are related physiologically and possibly genetically, researchers said in the statement.
The study's lead author, pediatric psychiatrist Tanya Murphy, said the protein marker also had been linked to Sydenhams chorea, a rare complication of common strep throat.

Murphy said it was too early to know whether some cases of childhood-onset obsessive-compulsive disorder and Tourette's may be related to strep throat. It may be coincidental that the illnesses share the same biological marker, she said.
